snippet.title: Building & Firing a 13th-Century Trebuchet (Siege Engine) 🏰🪨
snippet.description:
Long before gunpowder cannons arrived in Europe, the supreme monarch of battlefield artillery was the Counterweight Trebuchet (Blide / Tribok).

Introduced in the late 12th century and dominating 13th-century sieges (ca. 1250 AD), this titanic timber engine utilized gravitational potential energy to launch 80-kilogram limestone boulders over 250 meters to pulverize fortress walls.

Watch this complete experimental archaeology reconstruction: hewing massive oak trestle frames, casting lead ballast into the swinging hopper, winding down the 10-meter ash beam with twin spoked windlasses, rigging the rawhide sling, and striking the iron trigger to unleash catastrophic kinetic power!

📜 THE 13TH-CENTURY EXPERIMENTAL ARCHAEOLOGY RECONSTRUCTION:

• The Physics of Gravitational Potential Energy:
Unlike torsion catapults (mangonels) that stored tension in twisted rope bundles, the trebuchet relies on a counterweight ratio (typically 50:1). Dropping 4 to 6 tons of stone and lead over a short distance accelerates the long throwing arm to whip-like velocities.

• The Double-Pendulum Sling Advantage:
The rawhide and hemp sling acts as a second pivot point. As the beam rotates, the sling lags behind along the glide chute before accelerating and snapping over the apex, effectively doubling the projectile's launch velocity compared to a fixed-arm throwing cup.

• Heavy Timber Joinery & Drawboring:
A frame subject to repetitive multi-ton shockwaves cannot rely on iron nails. The trestle is assembled with deep mortise-and-tenon joints secured by faceted oak treenails (Holznägel), allowing the wood to flex and dissipate recoil without splitting.

• The Angled Release Prong:
The trajectory of the stone is governed entirely by the bent iron prong at the arm’s tip. A steeper forward angle delays ring release for a flatter trajectory against walls, while a straighter pin releases early for a high arc over castle towers.

• Sourcing Ballast (Lead & Granite):
To maximize weight within a compact wooden box, medieval siege engineers interleaved river boulders with melted lead pigs. Packing lead into the interstitial voids increased ballast density by nearly 40%, ensuring rapid acceleration.

snippet.title: How to grow lucky bamboo the right way!
snippet.description:
Lucky bamboo Care Guide Here: 

Soil: Use a well-draining potting mix. Regular houseplant mix with a little perlite works well. The pot needs a drainage hole.

Watering: Keep the soil lightly moist but never soggy. Water when the top inch feels dry, which is usually about once a week.

Water quality: It’s sensitive to the fluoride and chlorine in tap water, which cause yellow or brown tips. Use filtered, distilled, or rain water, or let tap water sit out overnight.

Light: Bright, indirect light. Direct sun scorches the leaves, and low light makes the stalks stretch and fade.

Temperature: 65–90°F. Keep it away from AC vents and drafts.

Fertilizer: Feed lightly with a diluted liquid houseplant fertilizer every 1–2 months in spring and summer. Too much burns the roots.

Humidity: Average indoor humidity is fine, but in dry Arizona air it’ll appreciate an occasional misting.

Switching from water to soil: Expect a few weeks of adjustment while the roots adapt. Keep the soil a bit wetter than usual during that time.

Pets: It’s toxic to cats and dogs, so keep it out of reach.

(Technically not even a bamboo, it’s a Dracaena)
